transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-01 15:30 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE); Aaron Patel (Lynx CTO), Rachel Kim (Lynx ML Eng), Tom Brewer (Lynx Infra), Nadia El-Khoury (Lynx Product)
---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick check-in on the pilot econ and throughput numbers. We ran the updated quantized model overnight; Diego you ran the bench, can you kick us off?
[00:18] Diego: Yeah, sure. So um, short version: with the 4-bit quant weight profile we saw tokens per second go up about 28% on the A100 pool, tokens per dollar improved roughly 22% when we factor in the slightly higher memory pressure. Those are... caveats, right, because we used synthetic shorter prompts.
[00:37] Aaron: Is that across the board or only for short seqs? Our production prompts skew long — 700 to 1k tokens.
[00:45] Diego: Good point. The gains are biggest at <=512 seq. For 1k sequences the improvement drops to about 10-12% due to KV cache misses and decoder overhead. We did a run with prefix caching enabled and that improved long-seq performance by another 6% tokens/sec.
[01:05] Rachel: Quick clarifying q — what do you mean by prefix caching? Are we caching the embedding states or the KV pairs?
[01:12] Diego: We're storing compressed KV cache snapshots for repeated conversation prefixes — so when the prompt shares a common intro we can reuse the KV state instead of recomputing. It's not a full embedding cache — more like a partial KV snapshot. In some transcripts the ASR messed up the acronym but it's KV.
[01:30] Tom: Latency-wise, enabling prefix cache added negligible overhead, but during high concurrency we saw CPU serialization on the host when inflating snapshots. Could be an IO pattern issue.
[01:45] Maya: Right, that's the tradeoff — caching yields unit cost savings but ops complexity. For Lynx's SLA you mentioned a 150ms p50 target?
[01:52] Nadia: We're targeting p50 ~120ms and p95 under 400ms for customer-facing features. Background batch jobs can be looser.
[02:01] Diego: With larger batching window we reduced cost per token because more requests batched, token/sec overall went up, but p95 spiked beyond 400ms if concurrency hit a particular shape. We tuned the batcher to prioritize low-latency routes and that helped bring p95 back in line but reduced batching efficiency by around 8%.
[02:21] Rachel: So concretely, tokens/sec/$ improved 18% with batching tuned for econ, but our p95 would exceed target unless we do route-level SLOs?
[02:30] Diego: Exactly. Route-level SLOs or partitioning customers onto a low-latency pool vs an econ pool. Redwood Dedicated could give you separate GPU pools but that implies reserved capacity and commit costs.
[02:44] Aaron: We're sensitive to committed spend. Can you show the delta between hosted autoscaled vs a small dedicated pool for our expected 3M tokens/day?
[02:54] Maya: We have a spreadsheet — I'll share. Short answer: hosted autoscale with caching+batching saves you capex early, dedicated gives slightly better p95 consistency and predictable unit cost at higher volume but you pay a baseline. For 3M tokens/day the break-even is around 6-8 months depending on cache hit rates.
[03:15] Tom: Network egress also changes the calculus — our infra team needs to know bytes out because that affects cloud cost. We'll send those numbers.
[03:22] Rachel: Another question — are the token counts normalized across model variants? We tested both the base 13B and a distilled 6B in parallel.
[03:30] Diego: We normalized to tokens generated not model parameters. The 6B had lower latency per token but worse quality on the generative tasks for you, so there's a tradeoff in quality vs cost. We suggested an A/B routing where deterministic responses use 6B and creative prompts use 13B.
[03:48] Nadia: For product success criteria, the main metric is user satisfaction score plus latency. If quality drops our retention may dip and the cost win won't matter.
[03:55] Maya: Totally. We'll tie quality regressions to the eval suite and set alerts. We can also do canary routing — start a subset of requests on the 6B and compare human evals.
[04:07] Aaron: On security, are there any additional obligations if we enable prefix caching? Does it store PII?
[04:14] Diego: Prefixed KV snapshots only contain model activations, not raw PII text, but if your prompts include PII then it's in the upstream context. We can apply redaction at ingest or configure TTLs and encryption on the cache snapshots. Redwood supports KMS-managed keys for Private deployments.
[04:32] Maya: I'll attach the security FAQ and the SOC2 summary in the follow-up.
[04:37] Rachel: Great. Back to numbers — can we get a simple metric: tokens/sec per dollar for three configs: (1) hosted + caching + tuned batching, (2) hosted default, (3) small dedicated pool with caching?
[04:49] Diego: We computed approximate numbers: (1) 0.00038 tokens/sec/$ per concurrent stream — actually per-dollar-per-hour normalized; (2) 0.00031; (3) 0.00042 but dedicated assumes 70% utilization to hit that. These are approximate and depend a lot on your hit rates and seq length.
[05:10] Aaron: The units are a bit confusing — can you convert to tokens per dollar per thousand requests or per 1M tokens/day?
[05:18] Maya: Yes, we'll convert to tokens per dollar per million tokens/day and post it.
[05:22] Diego: One more operational note: when we increased prefix cache TTL to 30m we saw hitrate jump from 18% to 46% for your sample set, which materially lowered compute. But snapshot inflation time increased and we had the CPU serialization at scale — Tom that aligns with what you saw.
[05:40] Tom: Yes — adding parallel decompression threads fixed some of it in the staging run but we need to tune the worker pool.
[05:47] Priya: For reproducibility, I'm going to add runbook steps: exact flags, sample prompts, the commands we used to collect p50/p95 and cost. I'll share that as a gist.
[05:57] Rachel: On quantization: quality drift shows up more in longer contexts. The hallucination rate ticked slightly up in the 4-bit profile for edge-case prompts. Did you try a hybrid quant (float for decoder)?
[06:08] Diego: We experimented with mixed precision: keep attention and output projection in FP16 and quantize feed-forward layers. That alleviated most drift but also reduces the pure tokens/sec gain; it's a middle ground.
[06:19] Nadia: Could we do dynamic routing based on prompt type? Quick deterministic outputs go to cheaper route, open-ended to higher-quality route?
[06:25] Maya: Absolutely — Redwood supports function-call routing and rules. We can build a classifier or simple heuristics and route accordingly. That usually gives the best unit economics without harming UX.
[06:37] Aaron: What's the effort to integrate that classifier?
[06:40] Diego: Lightweight — a small lambda that inspects prompt metadata, returns route tag. We'll provide code snippets.
[06:46] Maya: Alright, let's set concrete experiments for next week: 24h stress run with current batcher+cache, then re-run with the larger batch-window alpha and the prefix cache TTL tweak. Diego you'll collect p50/p95, tokens/sec, cache hitrate, and cost delta.
[07:03] Diego: Yep. Also we'll capture per-model quality metrics for the A/B. We'll add human eval samples for edge cases.
[07:10] Aaron: One last thing — pricing sensitivity: if we cross X tokens/day milestone do you have volume discounts?
[07:17] Maya: Yes, Redwood has tiered pricing and for pilots we can model a committed discount for the Dedicated option; we'll include scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[07:25] Rachel: Ok, thanks. Could you also include an example traffic shape we should simulate? Our live traffic has bursts every hour and long tails.
[07:33] Priya: We'll include a synthetic load generator config that reproduces burst + tail. It's a yaml we can paste into your harness.
[07:39] Tom: We'll also provide egress numbers by end of day tomorrow.
[07:43] Maya: Great. Anything else?
[07:45] Nadia: No, that's it from product.
[07:47] Aaron: Thanks all.
[07:49] Maya: Recap — Maya to send cost spreadsheet + security docs; Diego to tune batcher + caching and share results; Rachel/Tom to run stress test and give egress; follow-up sync target next week after the 24h run.
[07:59] Maya: Alright we'll wrap. Thanks everyone.
---
End transcript.
Notes: Occasional transcription errors in acronyms (KV vs. QV), filler words, and crosstalk present. References: cost spreadsheet link (will be shared), security FAQ link (redwood.com/security/lynx-faq), runbook gist (internal).
